Web Teardown
Product analysis · reconstruction specification

Block Burner

A browser-first competitive stacker with unusually legible tactical pressure—and a first-session teaching gap around matching, attacks and powerup causality.

PvP puzzle stackerCPU / local / onlineKeyboard-firstTwo complete rounds observedAI-assisted build claim

01
Executive verdict

Readable competition, under-explained causality.

Falling three-block pieces × colour matching × tactical powerups × opponent overload.

Observed The browser build reaches play quickly, supports a clean rematch, exposes both boards at once and makes rising danger visually obvious. The strongest quality is the shared tactical field: the player can see personal risk and the opponent’s state without opening another layer.

Hypothesis The weak point is not the mechanical premise but attribution. Matches vanish, debris flies, side-rail icons accumulate and special face blocks enter the board, yet the first session does not clearly explain which action caused which pressure event.

Study it — but rebuild the teaching layer

Best asset

Immediate competitive readability across two symmetrical grids.

Main risk

A novice can operate the piece but cannot reliably predict scoring, attack value, powerup timing or garbage consequences.

Product posture

Promising compact arcade system; evidence of retention, online liquidity and balance is absent.

03
What the game is

A simultaneous survival duel built from falling letter blocks.

Genre and perspective

Real-time competitive falling-block puzzle viewed from a fixed, front-on desktop layout. A human board sits left of an opponent board; both remain visible.

Session goal

Keep the player grid below the top boundary while matching blocks, scoring and applying enough pressure to overload the opponent first.

Fantasy

An arcade cabinet contest translated into the browser: quick rounds, glowing score readouts, chunky tiles and escalating visual chaos.

Observed mode

Single human versus CPU on Easy. Two rounds ended with Player Two winning.

Advertised breadth

CPU at four difficulty tiers, online multiplayer, local two-player on one keyboard and up to eight online slots.

Probable audience

Hypothesis Desktop puzzle players who value rapid rematches, visible mastery and asynchronous-to-synchronous social escalation.

04
Observed first session

The player learns operation quickly, but meaning arrives late.

1 · Entry

The landing page presents a prominent online CTA, four CPU difficulties, a learning route and local 2P. Easy CPU is selected.

2 · Ready gate

A centered “Ready to play?” dialog confirms “CPU: Easy” and offers Home or Start game. The board and controls remain visible behind it.

3 · First action

A vertical three-block piece appears. Arrow keys move, alter colour configuration and drop; the timer begins only after Start.

4 · First payoff

A matching group disappears and the score rises. The event is visually energetic, but no label explains match size or attack value.

5 · Pressure

Both grids accumulate irregular towers. Special-icon tiles and face-like obstacle blocks appear while scores climb independently.

6 · Failure

The human grid reaches an overload condition; a modal declares “Game Over” and “Player Two wins!”

7 · Rematch

Rematch immediately resets both boards and current scores while displaying the previous round values beside them.

8 · Furthest state

A second, longer round again ends in a CPU win. Returning home exposes the same mode menu and public score surface.

05
Core loop

Place, match, convert, pressure, survive.

Read

Inspect the falling three-block piece, the current stack and opponent danger.

Configure

Move horizontally and cycle the piece’s colours before commitment.

Drop

Send the piece down into a chosen column; blocks settle into the grid.

Resolve

Matching groups clear, score changes and animated debris communicates resolution.

Pressure

Specials, powerups or attack events alter one or both boards; exact conversion is only partly evidenced.

Survive

Repeat faster as stacks rise until one grid overloads, then rematch or exit.

Visible The repeat motive is a combined score race and survival race. Unknown Match geometry, attack tables, spawn distribution, combo window and difficulty scaling were not exhaustively demonstrated.

Camera

Fixed orthographic UI; no pan, zoom or pointer aiming. Critical play stays in the central dual-grid stage.

Focus and keyboard safety

Implementation choice Capture arrows and Space only while the game has focus; prevent page scroll; show a focus-lost pause.

Accessibility gap

Colour and letters overlap as redundant signals, which helps; however, powerup icons lack explanatory labels during play and no alternate bindings were observed.

The board tells us the systems; it does not reveal every formula.

08
Progression, economy and content

Round mastery is visible; durable progression is mostly a promise.

Within-round progression

Score, combo potential, powerup inventory, incoming obstacles and stack height all create escalating tactical state.

Between-round continuity

Rematch preserves each side’s previous score in compact badges while resetting boards, timer and current scores.

Persistent statistics

The landing page says a free account keeps statistics; no account flow or saved profile was opened.

Leaderboard

Public columns include username, high score, highest combo, blocks burned and playtime. Copy states that player-reported scores update after matches end.

Content breadth

Four CPU tiers and three play routes are visible. Additional boards, cosmetics, seasons or rule sets were not shown.

Monetization

Unknown The game is presented as free; no purchase, ad, premium tier or virtual currency surfaced.

Expansion cost: medium. New difficulty profiles and powerups reuse the grid, but every added effect multiplies balance, telegraphing and multiplayer synchronization demands. Content is cheap to draw and expensive to make fair.
09
UX/UI reconstruction atlas

Four observed screen families define the build.

Desktop evidence is strong. Narrow-screen behavior is unknown and should not be represented as original behavior.

A · Landing and mode selection

Purpose
Explain fantasy, select route and surface social proof.
Composition
Centered max-width panel; brand and aggregate counters above a two-column hero; modes left, high scores right; product copy below.
Visible copy
“Free to play — no download or install required.” “PLAY ONLINE MULTIPLAYER.” “Play against CPU.” “LEARN TO PLAY.” “START: 2P (SAME KEYBOARD).”
Actions
Online, Easy, Hard, Beast Mode, Insane, Learn, local 2P, story and footer links.
States
Default, hover/focus, data loading/error, leaderboard empty/populated and signed-in/out are required; only populated/default is visible.

B · Match shell and ready dialog

Purpose
Confirm mode while teaching controls before simulation starts.
Composition
Brand top-left; home/pause/menu controls above the left grid; timer centered; score labels above both grids; legends left; additional-player rail right.
Visible copy
“Ready to play?” “CPU: Easy. Start when you’re ready.” “Home.” “Start game.”
Modal behavior
Background visible but inert. Start begins timer and piece spawn; Home exits.
Accessibility
Focus starts on Start game; Escape should return safely; all underlying controls are removed from tab order.

C · Active match

Purpose
Support simultaneous placement, self-risk reading and opponent surveillance.
Composition
Two equal tall grids share a center seam; each has an active-piece lane and a narrow side inventory. Scores sit directly above ownership labels.
Persistent UI
Timer, current scores, previous scores, mode label, controls, navigation, queues and dormant slots for players three through eight.
Local feedback
Block glow, icon badges, matched-block debris, score change, settling and obstacle sprites.
Required states
Spawning, falling, cycling, blocked, locking, resolving, combo, attack pending, powerup ready/empty, danger, paused and focus lost.

D · Result and rematch

Purpose
Stop simulation, declare winner and offer the shortest replay route.
Composition
Dimmed/frozen match remains visible; centered translucent panel with title, winner, primary gradient button and secondary home action.
Visible copy
“Game Over.” “Player Two wins!” “Rematch.” “Back to homepage.”
Transition
Rematch clears boards, resets current scores and timer, and transfers last-round scores to “Previous.”
Missing
No cause-of-loss, score breakdown, combo summary or powerup report.

10
Feedback and presentation

Impact is abundant; explanation is scarce.

Strong feedback

  • Matched blocks tumble away as physical debris.
  • Scores update in large badges near player labels.
  • Special tiles carry unmistakable icon overlays.
  • Result modal freezes and dims the entire arena.
  • Small particles create an arcade-finale feel.

Ambiguous feedback

  • No attack-value label links a clear to opponent pressure.
  • Obstacle origin is not called out.
  • Powerup icon meanings are not named in play.
  • Danger lacks a dedicated top-out meter.
  • Larger score jumps have no inline breakdown.

Audio boundary

Unknown No reliable sound vocabulary is established by the visual materials. A reconstruction should map spawn, move, lock, clear, combo, attack, warning and result to distinct cues, then validate separately.

11
Social, viral and return loops

The product advertises breadth before proving liquidity.

Immediate return loop

Prominent Rematch, previous-score memory, fast reset and short survival rounds create a clean “one more” structure.

Mastery loop

Placement efficiency, colour cycling, combo construction, word completion, powerup timing and opponent reading can support skill depth.

Social loop

Online, same-keyboard play and a visible eight-player capacity create challenge potential. None of those paths were completed in this session.

Status loop

High score, highest combo, blocks burned and playtime expose multiple bragging dimensions beyond win/loss.

Shareability

Hypothesis Late-round board chaos and the “BURNER” special event are the strongest clip moments; no native share action was visible.

Retention boundary

No daily goals, unlock track, season, streak, friend graph or durable reward loop was observed. Their absence from evidence is not proof they never exist.

12
Strengths and frictions

The foundations are good enough to make the missing explanations costly.

What works

  • Fast mode selection: CPU play is one click from the landing page.
  • Preflight clarity: difficulty and controls are visible before Start.
  • Spatial honesty: both boards use equal visual weight.
  • Readable danger: stack height directly communicates risk.
  • Replay speed: result → rematch → active play is compact.
  • Identity: dark green cabinet styling differentiates the familiar mechanic.

What blocks understanding

  • P0 Match rule and valid geometry are not stated in the active shell.
  • P0 Attacks, garbage and powerups lack source→effect attribution.
  • P1 Result screen does not explain the overload cause or scoring.
  • P1 “BURNER” rule names a reward but not orientation or completion state.
  • P1 Side-rail icons are visually distinct but semantically unlabeled.
  • P2 Empty P3–P8 slots consume substantial width in a two-player CPU match.

Development story and technology

One concrete AI claim; almost every runtime detail remains unknown.

Team

Creator source Radar maps the release post to RainDust. The site footer credits “Created By: Justin Stewart.” Whether those labels identify the same person was not independently verified.

Timeline

The linked creator post claims an eleven-hour continuous build session before the 17 September 2026 release.

Confirmed tool

ChatGPT Pro is named as development assistance and the creator mentions exhausting a weekly limit. This does not identify the runtime stack.

Playable surface

playblockburner.com hosts the browser version represented in the recording.

Unverified stack

Engine, language, frontend framework, networking model, database, hosting, art tooling and audio tooling are not established by the checked sources.

Process and iteration

No repository, commit history, workflow breakdown, named challenge or post-feedback iteration was documented in the Radar snapshot.

Do not over-read the AI claim. ChatGPT Pro is a confirmed development aid, not proof of generated art, generated code percentage, autonomous creation, model version, backend architecture or production quality.

Reconstruction blueprint

Rebuild causality before adding content.

Screen state machine

Landing→Mode selected→Ready→Active match↔Paused→Game Over→Rematch / Home

Resolution pipeline

Spawn triad→Move / cycle→Drop / lock→Find matches→Clear / score→Special / attack→Gravity→Overflow check

Minimum data model

EntityRequired fieldsInvariant
GameSessionmode, difficulty, status, elapsed, roundId, playerSlotsSimulation advances only while status is active.
PlayerStateslot, type, currentScore, previousScore, combo, danger, connectedOwnership is explicit for every score and attack.
Gridwidth, height, cells, activePiece, overflowStateOne settled block per cell; active piece never mutates settled data.
Blockid, letter, colour, specialType, obstacleType, stateVisual identity derives from data, not DOM position.
Pieceblocks[3], column, row, cycleIndex, fallStateOrdering is deterministic through colour cycles.
ResolutionmatchedCells, chainIndex, scoreDelta, generatedAttack, spawnedRewardEvery visible change has a cause recorded in one transaction.
Poweruptype, charges, source, targetPolicy, stateUnavailable effects cannot consume input.
AttacksourcePlayer, targetPlayer, amount, payload, telegraphStateSender, target and pending consequence are inspectable.
LeaderboardEntrydisplayName, highScore, highestCombo, blocksBurned, playtimeServer validates submissions; display names are escaped.

Mandatory behavior

Deterministic match core

  • Seed piece generation for replayable tests.
  • Lock, match, clear, gravity and chain resolve in stable order.
  • CPU uses the same legal action contract as a human.
  • Game Over stops all timers and queued actions.

Causal feedback

  • Label clear size, combo, score delta and attack delta.
  • Telegraph incoming garbage before it lands.
  • Name powerups on earn and activation.
  • Show why the terminal overflow occurred.

Network boundary

  • Implementation choice Server-authoritative lock and resolution for online play.
  • Reconnect, timeout, empty-lobby and host-loss states are explicit.
  • Never treat client-reported leaderboard data as authoritative.
  • Offline CPU remains available when matchmaking fails.

Unknown content boundary

  • Do not invent Hard, Beast Mode or Insane AI parameters.
  • Do not infer eight-player board layout from dormant thumbnails.
  • Do not assign unseen effects to icon art.
  • Gate unobserved account/statistics behavior behind interfaces.

Vertical slices

1 · Solo board

Spawn, move, cycle, drop, lock, match, score and overflow with deterministic fixtures.

2 · Duel shell

Two boards, CPU Easy, timer, current/previous scores, ready and result states.

3 · Specials

4 · Social shell

17
Acceptance specification

Prove the duel, the attribution and the reset.

First entry. Given a fresh visitor, when the page loads, then brand, free-to-play copy, online CTA, four CPU tiers, learning route, local 2P and populated-or-valid-empty leaderboard states appear without overflow.
Choose Easy. Given the landing page, when Easy is activated, then the dual-grid shell opens with the correct control legend and a modal confirming “CPU: Easy.”
Start gate. Given the ready modal, when Start game is activated, then focus moves to the playfield, the modal closes, the timer starts and both sides receive legal pieces.
Move boundaries. Given an active piece at either wall, when the player moves farther outward, then the piece remains in bounds and no settled cell changes.
Colour cycle. Given a three-block piece, when Up is pressed repeatedly, then its colour order cycles deterministically and returns to its initial arrangement after a full cycle.
Drop and lock. Given a legal column, when Down is pressed, then the triad descends, settles above occupied cells and triggers exactly one resolution transaction.
Basic clear. Given the minimum valid matching group, when the piece locks, then only the eligible group clears, debris plays, score delta is shown and gravity resolves before the next spawn.
Invalid non-match. Given adjacent tiles that do not satisfy the rule, when resolution runs, then they remain, score stays unchanged and no attack is generated.
BURNER reward. Given a configuration that satisfies the explicitly configured word rule, when it resolves, then the earned powerup is named, added to the correct rail and announced once.
Powerup use. Given one available charge, when Space is pressed, then one charge is consumed and source, target and effect are visibly attributable; with zero charges, input is a safe no-op.
Incoming pressure. Given an opponent-generated attack, when it is queued, then the target sees a warning and payload before obstacle placement; applying it cannot overwrite occupied cells silently.
Pause / resume. Given an active round, when Pause is activated, then timer, gravity, CPU and input freeze; Resume restores the exact state without duplicate ticks.
Overflow result. Given no valid spawn space after resolution, when overflow is confirmed, then simulation freezes and Game Over names the opposite player as winner.
Rematch. Given Game Over, when Rematch is activated, then both grids, timer, current scores, queues and inventories reset while previous scores retain the final round values.
Home exit. Given the result modal, when Back to homepage is activated, then the landing page returns and no stale gameplay listener captures arrow keys.
Visual regression. At wide desktop width, compare landing, ready, sparse match, danger, result and rematch states for dual-grid symmetry, icon legibility, modal focus, timer placement and zero horizontal clipping.
18
Experiments

Make mastery legible before increasing spectacle.

1 · First-clear coach

Hypothesis: one contextual overlay that previews a valid three-block match will reduce early random dropping.

Test: compare current shell with a one-time ghost highlight and “Match 3+ of one colour” label.

Success: higher first-clear completion and fewer drops before first score.

False read: faster clears may come from a lucky opening seed.

2 · Attack receipt

Hypothesis: “You sent 2” / “2 incoming” receipts will turn chaos into strategy.

Test: add source-coloured arrows and a brief pending payload badge.

Success: more correct explanations of why garbage appeared; higher rematch rate.

False read: novelty animation can improve ratings without improving comprehension.

3 · Result debrief

Hypothesis: a compact breakdown will strengthen mastery and soften unexplained losses.

Test: add largest clear, highest combo, powerups used, pressure sent and loss cause above Rematch.

Success: faster rematch decision and more second-round starts.

False read: an extra screen may delay players who already understand the game.

4 · Empty-lobby fallback

Hypothesis: immediate CPU substitution preserves intent when online liquidity is low.

Test: after a short search, offer “Play CPU while we keep looking.”

Success: fewer homepage returns and more completed first rounds.

False read: CPU play may mask weak multiplayer demand rather than solve it.

5 · Focused 2P shell

Hypothesis: hiding dormant P3–P8 slots in CPU and local 2P increases board readability without weakening multiplayer positioning.

Test: collapse the right rail behind a “Modes up to 8 players” badge.

Success: improved first-session rule recall and fewer missed danger events.

False read: more board area can itself improve performance independently of comprehension.

19
Confidence and unknowns

High confidence in CPU Easy; low confidence outside it.

High confidence

  • Landing hierarchy and visible mode choices.
  • Ready, active, Game Over and rematch states.
  • Keyboard controls displayed in the shell.
  • Dual-grid composition, score and previous-score behavior.
  • Two completed CPU Easy rounds and winner copy.
  • Leaderboard columns and free-account promise.

Medium confidence

  • Matching requires at least three same-colour blocks.
  • Special tiles feed a side-rail powerup system.
  • Face blocks represent opponent pressure or garbage.
  • Larger resolutions create combos and stronger attacks.
  • Site credit and creator handle may identify one person.

Unknown

  • Exact match geometry and score formula.
  • Every powerup effect and BURNER reward rule.
  • Hard, Beast Mode and Insane behavior.
  • Online matchmaking, latency, reconnects and eight-player layout.
  • Local 2P controls and account flow.
  • Leaderboard validation and persistence.
  • Sound design, mobile support and complete runtime stack.

Evidence boundary

Observed The first-session path, two CPU rounds, controls, results and rematch behavior come from the recorded interaction states. Visible Exact interface copy, layout, scores, icons and landing claims come from the product screens. Radar Launch metrics, creator attribution, date and AI-development claim come from the dated creator-source snapshot. Hypothesis Audience fit, growth drivers, recommended implementation choices and experiments are interpretations. Unknown Unseen modes and formulas are deliberately not reconstructed as facts.

Bottom line. Block Burner is reconstruction-ready as a CPU Easy vertical slice. A faithful online or advanced-difficulty recreation requires direct evidence of matchmaking, one human-versus-human round, powerup definitions, attack conversion, pause/menu behavior, account persistence and mobile input.
